references.text: The same chapter describes how the sea covered the Egyptians and they sank like lead in the mighty waters, paralleling sinking like a stone into the depths.
Nehemiah refers to this event and uses similar language about the pursuers being cast into the depths like stones in mighty waters.
The psalm describes how the sea overwhelmed the enemies, a poetic retelling of the Egyptians' destruction at the Red Sea.
The psalm states that the water covered the opponents and not one of them was left, reflecting תְּהֹמֹת יְכַסְיֻמוּ.
Describes how Pharaoh and his army were cast into the Red Sea, a reference to the same event.
Uses similar imagery about sinking into the depths of the sea (מִמְּצוּלוֹת מָיִם), which corresponds with בִמְצוֹלֹת.
Jonah describes how the deep (תְּהוֹם) surrounded him, using similar vocabulary about the depths of the sea.
Uses an identical metaphor of 'staggering like a drunkard' to illustrate total helplessness without God's intervention.
Psalm 107:26 is a direct poetic reflection on the Red Sea event in Exodus, focusing on the 'deep' as the arena of judgment.
A thematic parallel about God's judgment tearing away the enemy's foundation and existence (water versus river imagery).
Uses the same metaphor of 'reeling like a drunkard' to depict helplessness under God's judgment (the process in Job versus the result in Exodus).
